$comment: Why each family is in the pool, and who said so. data/pool.json decides WHAT the season grades; this file records WHY that choice is defensible, with a citation per claim. It exists because the pool's own justification was mechanical - a scenario was in because some benchmark author had banded it - and 'an author put it in a tier' does not answer 'is this a good measure of dynamic clicking'. Nothing reads this at runtime: it is documentation held to the same standard as code, which is what npm run validate:rationale is for. Every number quoted here is re-derived from data/scenario_taxonomy.json rather than trusted, and every family in the pool must appear.
$evidence: Three kinds, in descending order of what they can settle. A benchmark author's published design note is the strongest: it says what the scenario was built to isolate, in the words of the person who built it. KovaaK's own in-game scenario description is next, and is first-party for scenarios no benchmark documents. Community discussion is last and is used only where it says something the other two do not - which is mostly about scenarios that predate the benchmarks that later adopted them. Where a family's evidence is thin, this file says so rather than padding it: 'thin' is a fact about the pool worth being able to see.
$audience: plays and entries are KovaaK's own counters for the named scenario, copied from data/scenario_taxonomy.json and checked against it. They are here because 'the community plays this' is a claim that should carry a number. Read entries as people who have posted a score and plays as runs; the least-played scenario in the pool has 13,262 plays, so nothing here is obscure.

families.isolates: Leading a small target that changes direction, where the shot has to be placed ahead of it.
families.why: The angelic bot, which drifts rather than strafes, so the lead is continuous instead of stepped. No single author cut it at four difficulties; psalmTS and Pasu each cut it at two, and the four ascend across them.

families.isolates: Clicking a target that reverses through 180 degrees, so the lead has to be re-aimed mid-flick.
families.why: A target that reverses through 180 degrees, which is the sharpest lead-change in the sub-skill. Voltaic's two cuts then Revosect's two, ascending across the pair. B180 rAim Easy is Revosect's Easy cut and sat at Advanced, above B180 Voltaic, which Voltaic grades Advanced and Jade Palace grades Easy. Two sheets put the standard cut above the easy one and the ladder had them the other way round, so the two are swapped.

families.isolates: Switching between static spheres that have to be drilled rather than clicked, so the aim has to hold through the kill.
families.why: Hand-built into Static Clicking over two hours and moved here on a measurement, not a preference. All four rungs fire a Poke-Drill at 22.1, 27.7, 31.8 and 54.4 shots per kill across 119 runs of the corpus; the 191 correctly-labelled clicking scenarios sit between 1.0 and 1.3, so a single click kills nothing here and the family cannot be clicking of any kind. KovaaK's types all sixteen Pokeball scenarios in the corpus as Switching, and the benchmark labels land eight of them on Speed Switching - AimSpeed, Viscose, Avasive and Revosect - against two Lemon calls Stability. The rungs are unchanged from the Static Clicking build.

That is the opposite of how the other static families are assembled and it is why two of its four rungs are hand-picked. What it isolates is real and not covered elsewhere: at these target sizes the limit is the tremor in the stop, not the speed of the travel.

The easy rung is the lineage author's own supereasy cut, made for people who cannot yet hold the graded ones, which is exactly what a Novice rung is for.

families.why: The one family in the pool no benchmark sheet grades at any difficulty, and it is here because that absence is a gap rather than a verdict. Raw click speed on targets a player can already hit is a thing the community tests constantly and the sheets do not cover, so all four rungs are picked and the family is documented as thin. 1wall9000targets is the reference scenario for it and carries a larger board than most graded scenarios in this season.

evidence.says: 108,729 players have posted a score on it, which is a larger board than most graded scenarios in this season carry - the absence of a benchmark tier is not an absence of an audience.

families.thin: No benchmark sheet grades this lineage at any difficulty, so there is no design note to cite and the family rests on the pool's own reading of the test. That is a fact about the sheets rather than the scenario, and it is recorded here rather than papered over.

Three fixed points rather than a line: the return path is graded as well as the outward one, which is what separates it from Horizontal. TSK Mixed is the only sheet that carries ClickTrack at all, and it names its tiers after categories rather than difficulties, so the rungs are ordered by the lineage's own axis and not by a published tier.

families.isolates: Static clicking over long travel, at a sensitivity the scenario itself argues against lowering.
families.why: Two claims have to hold for a static family: that it measures clicking rather than pathing, and that it does not quietly reward a sensitivity nobody plays at. Voltaic built ww5t for the second, and the Wide Wall lineage above it is the oldest and most-played static test in the game - more evidence about what a static score means than any benchmark can supply. Its Novice rung comes from Avasive, a sheet this pool deliberately does not name as a source, so it is admitted on the shape of the test rather than on Avasive's grading.
